L0@P0: Quotient for Assume-Guarantee Contracts
L1@P0: Íñigo Íncer Romeo1, Alberto Sangiovanni-Vincentelli1, Chung-Wei Lin2, and Eunsuk Kang3
L2@P0: 1 University of California, Berkeley
L3@P0: {inigo, alberto}@eecs.berkeley.edu
L4@P0: 2 National Taiwan University
L5@P0: cwlin@csie.ntu.edu.tw
L6@P0: 3 Carnegie Mellon University
L7@P0: eskang@cmu.edu
L8@P0: Abstract—We introduce a novel notion of quotient set for a
L9@P0: pair of contracts and the operation of quotient for assumeguarantee contracts. The quotient set and its related operation
L10@P0: can be used in any compositional methodology where design
L11@P0: requirements are mapped into a set of components in a library.
L12@P0: In particular, they can be used for the so called missing component problem, where the given components are not capable
L13@P0: of discharging the obligations of the requirements. In this case,
L14@P0: the quotient operation identifies the contract for a component
L15@P0: that, if added to the original set, makes the resulting system
L16@P0: fulfill the requirements.
L17@P0: 1. Introduction
L18@P0: Contracts have been proposed as a formal mechanism
L19@P0: to support compositional design first for complex software
L20@P0: (e.g., see [1] and references therein) and later for system
L21@P0: design (e.g., see [2] and references therein). We embed our
L22@P0: contribution on contracts in reuse-based, meet-in-the-middle
L23@P0: design methodologies such as Platform-Based Design (e.g.,
L24@P0: see [3]). In these methodologies that are fairly common
L25@P0: in industry, during the top-down phase, the specification
L26@P0: for a system is decomposed into a set of refined specifications of sub-components, i.e., the high-level architecture
L27@P0: of the design is determined. This step fits in a refinement
L28@P0: driven process where higher level specifications are mapped
L29@P0: into lower level implementations. This decomposition is
L30@P0: “guided” by the existence of a set of predefined components
L31@P0: in a library, the bottom-up part of the methodology.
L32@P0: More formally, suppose a designer wishes to implement
L33@P0: a system that satisfies a top-level specification T , and will
L34@P0: use in this design a set of n components from a library
L35@P0: with specifications F =(Ti)n
L36@P0: i=1. If the composition of
L37@P0: these n design elements refines the top level specification
L38@P0: T , the design assembled from the components satisfies the
L39@P0: specification. However, if this is not the case, the designer
L40@P0: must add at least one element to the library. In other words,
L41@P0: the designer must identify a specification TM such that its
L42@P0: composition with the composition of (Ti)n
L43@P0: i=1 refines T .
L44@P0: This problem corresponds to identifying the missing (unknown) component in a library (e.g., see [4] and references
L45@P0: therein). In the language of contract-based design, we need
L46@P0: to compute the contract quotient that guarantees that TM
L47@P0: is as “large” a specification as possible in the refinement
L48@P0: order so that whoever is in charge of adding the element to
L49@P0: Lin and Kang were at Toyota ITC U.S.A. Inc., when this work was done.
L50@P0: the library has the maximum degree of freedom in its implementation. In industry, this problem is in general tackled
L51@P0: heuristically. Our proposed notion of quotient for assumeguarantee contracts aims at finding a rigorous procedure for
L52@P0: the determination of the largest specification of the missing
L53@P0: component.
L54@P0: Related work. In [5], Le et al. address the problem of fixing
L55@P0: a decomposition so that it refines a specification: given a
L56@P0: top-level contract C and family of contracts (Ci)n
L57@P0: i=1 whose
L58@P0: composition may not refine C, find a family (C0

L64@P0: the designer begins with a high-level specification C and
L65@P0: an initial decomposition of the specification into various

L69@P0: Notions similar to quotients have been previously investigated in the context of various behavioral formalisms.
L70@P0: Chilton et al. formulate in [6] an assume-guarantee framework for reasoning about components modeled as a variant
L71@P0: of interface automata introduced by Chen et al. [7], including quotient operations. Similarly, Bhaduri and Ramesh [8]
L72@P0: investigate the problem of synthesizing, given P and Q as
L73@P0: interface automata, R such that the composition of R and
L74@P0: P refines Q; they provide a game-theoretic formulation of
L75@P0: the problem as computing winning strategies over a game
L76@P0: between P and Q. In addition, Raclet [9] introduces the
L77@P0: concept of a residual specification in the context of modal
L78@P0: automata.
L79@P0: Another related line of research is on assumption generation in the context of compositional verification [10]–
L80@P0: [12]: Given a component M and a desired property P, what
L81@P0: is the weakest assumption A that M can make about its
L82@P0: environment such that M  A |= P? These works typically
L83@P0: assume M and A to be labelled transition systems, and
L84@P0: exploit their structures as part of a learning algorithm (e.g.,
L85@P0: L* [13]).
L86@P0: Compared to the contributions mentioned above, our
L87@P0: approach differs in that we provide a general form for
L88@P0: the contract quotient for assume-guarantee contracts, i.e., a
L89@P0: formulation that holds for all variants of assume-guarantee
L90@P0: contracts. Furthermore, as far as we know, our approach is
L91@P0: the first to introduce the notion of a quotient set, which
L92@P0: defines a range of contracts that can be composed with C1
L93@P0: to yield the largest contract that refines C.
L94@P0: Specific Contributions. Benveniste et al. in their comprehensive review of contract based design [2], on page
L95@P0: 188, state that “no Least Upper Bound and no quotient are
L96@P0-1: 978-1-5386-6195-6/18/$31.00 c 2018 IEEEknown for A/G contracts.” One of our contributions is an
L97@P1: explicit form for the quotient operation of A/G contracts
L98@P1: (Theorem 3.5 in Section 3). We point out that notions
L99@P1: similar to quotients have been proposed for A/G contracts
L100@P1: before, but these operations are defined when contracts are
L101@P1: expressed in specific formalisms [6], [10], [14]. To the best
L102@P1: of our knowledge, the quotient operation for general A/G
L103@P1: contracts has not been addressed.
L104@P1: We also introduce the notion of the quotient set (Definition 3.6), a set that contains all contracts C0 such that
L105@P1: C0 ⌦ C1 =(C/C1) ⌦ C1 for given contracts C and C1. The
L106@P1: quotient set tells us which contracts extend C1 into C in the
L107@P1: largest way possible. We fully characterize the quotient set
L108@P1: in Theorem 3.7 (Section 3).
L109@P1: A further contribution of our paper is an alternate definition of the quotient operation for the meta-theory of
L110@P1: contracts (Section 4). The new definition makes the quotient
L111@P1: operation an obvious dual of the composition operation
L112@P1: and makes the derivation of the quotient for A/G contracts
L113@P1: almost immediate.
L114@P1: Finally, we show a methodology and examples of the use
L115@P1: of the quotient operation in the design of an ALU and of an
L116@P1: automotive system (Section 5). We believe the theory in this
L117@P1: paper can significantly improve the integration process in
L118@P1: practical system design. For example, it can assist automotive Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) in defining
L119@P1: the specification of a component to be implemented1. We
L120@P1: show that with appropriate automation tools, which are left
L121@P1: as future work, the process can be formal but still efficient.
L122@P1: 2. Contract-Based Design
L123@P1: Contract-based design (CBD) [15] has emerged as a
L124@P1: formal methodology for system-level design (see [2]
L125@P1: for a comprehensive analysis of the state-of-the-art). This
L126@P1: methodology supports open systems and the ability to fuse
L127@P1: multiple viewpoints in a single component. The former is
L128@P1: needed to support independent design, and the later to enable
L129@P1: the independent characterization of complementary aspects
L130@P1: of the same component (e.g., functionality and timing). At
L131@P1: the core of the contract algebra lies the notion of a component. Components are described by their IO connectivity and
L132@P1: by their dynamics. A specification, or contract, has semantics given by a pair (E,M) of sets of components which are,
L133@P1: respectively, environments for the contract and of components which are implementations for the contract. Contracts
L134@P1: provide a designer with (i) formal notions of refinement (to
L135@P1: enable substitution of components) and parallel composition
L136@P1: (to enable merging multiple components into one); (ii) the
L137@P1: ability to check compatibility between the objects to be
L138@P1: composed; and (iii) a formal means of communication of
L139@P1: requirements to suppliers. With a contract, a supplier has
L140@P1: all the required information to implement a subsystem in a
L141@P1: way which guarantees system integration.
L142@P1: 1. In industrial designs, OEMs generally keep most of the components
L143@P1: and only change as few components as possible when a new design is
L144@P1: developed. The task here is to perform the minimum amount of work
L145@P1: needed to identify and implement the new components
L146@P1: To be able to manipulate contracts, we need to assume more structure in them. Thus, there exist two specialized contract theories: interface theories and the assumeguarantee framework, our focus in this paper. In the assumeguarantee theory, components are modeled as sets of behaviors, where behaviors are successive assignments of values
L147@P1: to the various variables in the modeling framework (which
L148@P1: also determines the granularity of this succession: discrete,
L149@P1: continuous, asynchronous, etc.). For instance, if a designer
L150@P1: is implementing synchronous digital logic, his modeling
L151@P1: framework uses a discrete-event model of computation,
L152@P1: where behaviors are infinite, discrete sequences of values for
L153@P1: all variables under consideration. More concretely, suppose
L154@P1: we are dealing with only two boolean variables a and b; one
L155@P1: possible behavior is a b, a ¬b, ¬a ¬b, a b . . . If the designer is
L156@P1: implementing a cyber-physical system, his modeling framework may need to enable analysis of continuous dynamics.
L157@P1: An assume-guarantee contract C is given by a pair
L158@P1: (A, G), where A and G are, respectively, sets of behaviors for assumptions and for guarantees. In other words,
L159@P1: assumptions and guarantees are properties, sets of traces,
L160@P1: and thus can be expressed in any formal language, such as
L161@P1: LTL, MTL, and STL (e.g., [16]–[18]). This means that A/G
L162@P1: contracts are very flexible. We say a component M satisfies
L163@P1: a contract if it provides the contract guarantees subject to the
L164@P1: contract assumptions, i.e., if M ✓ G[¬A. With this notion
L165@P1: of satisfaction of an A/G contract, many A/G contract pairs
L166@P1: (A, G) can have the same semantics. In order to deal with
L167@P1: unique objects, we use contracts in saturated form. We say
L168@P1: contract C is saturated if G = G [ ¬A. Saturated contracts
L169@P1: have a maximal set of guarantees.
L170@P1: The algebra of contracts defines an order relation called
L171@P1: refinement and a binary operation called composition. Refinement allows designers to substitute a component with
L172@P1: another that has at least the same capabilities. This order
L173@P1: is defined as follows: let C0 =(A0,G0) and C =(A, G) be
L174@P1: saturated contracts. Contract C0 refines C, written C0  C,
L175@P1: if G0 ✓ G and A ✓ A0. Refinement amounts to weakening assumptions and strengthening guarantees. The binary
L176@P1: operation of composition produces a contract which represents the simultaneous operation of the two given contracts: let C00 =(A00,G00) be a saturated contract. Given C0
L177@P1: and C00, the binary operation ⌦ generates a new contract
L178@P1: C0 ⌦ C00 =(A0 \ A00 [ ¬G0 [ ¬G00,G0 \ G00). This is
L179@P1: usually called the horizontal composition of the contracts
L180@P1: C0 and C00. The composite of two contracts is required
L181@P1: to provide the guarantees of both; the composite assumes
L182@P1: simultaneously the assumptions of C0 and of C00 but relaxes
L183@P1: these assumptions by the guarantees of both C0 and C00. This
L184@P1: relaxation occurs because the guarantees of each contract
L185@P1: may help the to meet the other’s assumptions.
L186@P1: Refinement and composition allows us to discuss the
L187@P1: binary operation of quotient, a central topic of this paper.
L188@P1: The quotient between contracts C and C1, expressed C/C1,
L189@P1: is defined as
L190@P1-2: C0  C/C1 () C0 ⌦ C1  C. (1)The quotient provides the largest contract in the refinement order that, when composed with C1, refines C. The
L191@P2: explicit formulation of the quotient is not known for A/G
L192@P2: contracts [2]. One of our key contributions is the explicit
L193@P2: expression for this quotient.
L194@P2: 3. Quotient of Assume-Guarantee Contracts
L195@P2: Assume that C =(A, G) is the top-level specification
L196@P2: we wish to implement and that C1 =(A1,G1) is the
L197@P2: specification of a component that will be used in the design.
L198@P2: We are interested in the part of the specification that is not
L199@P2: discharged by C1, and in the maximal specification we can
L200@P2: form by composing C1 with a missing specification with
L201@P2: the result refining C. We introduce the quotient operation of
L202@P2: assume-guarantee contracts in Section 3.1. We introduce in

L204@P2: expresses what we need to do to complement C1 to satisfy
L205@P2: C in a maximal way in the refinement order. Theorems 3.5

L207@P2: provides an explicit formula for the quotient operation for

L294@P3: 3.2. Quotient Set of A/G Contracts
L295@P3: We introduce the concept of quotient set to answer two
L296@P3: questions:
L297@P3: • When designing a system to meet a specification C,
L298@P3: what is the biggest specification achievable if a component
L299@P3: with specification C1 must be used in the design? That is,
L300@P3: we seek to characterize the contracts whose compositions
L301@P3: with C1 result in the biggest possible contract that refines C.
L302@P3: • Given a contract C1 and a contract C that is the result
L303@P3: of the composition of C1 with another contract, what are all
L304@P3: contracts C0 that satisfy C = C1 ⌦ C0? In this case, we solve
L305@P3: the inverse problem to composition.
L306@P3: We call the set of such contracts the quotient set. We
L307@P3: begin our quest for the quotient set with an observation:
L308@P3: suppose that C0 is a saturated contract that satisfies C0 ⌦
L309@P3: C1  C. Then C0  C/C1. This last statement implies that
L310@P3: C0 ⌦ C1  C/C1 ⌦ C1. Thus, the greatest resulting contract
L311@P3: achievable by composing C1 with a contract with the result
L312@P3: refining C is C1 ⌦ C/C1. A quick computation reveals that
L313@P3: C1 ⌦ C/C1 =(A [ ¬G1,G1 \ (A1 \ G [ ¬A)).
